definition: The time and effort required for a user to become proficient with a new software tool or platform.
extendedDefinition: The learning curve is the time and effort users need to reach proficiency with a new tool, and it is one of the most under-budgeted costs in software adoption. Steep learning curves delay time-to-value, drain productivity during transition, and increase abandonment risk, especially for teams with limited training capacity. Buyers should estimate the curve for their specific users, since the same product can be fast for administrators and slow for casual end users. Signals to evaluate include guided setup, task-based documentation, sample data, and the vendor's training library. Rollout planning should stage adoption by role, starting with the groups that gain immediate value and learn quickly. Measuring the curve after launch, through activation rates and support volume, identifies where additional training is needed. Tools with gentle learning curves consistently deliver faster returns and lower total cost of ownership.
